cards.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers

United says sharing credentials may expose **sensitive information** or lead to **unintended purchases**; it also says AI check-ins could violate rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances. cards.title: Gemini Decisions API

depth.text: Google's new **decision API** scores questions about text, images, audio, video, and PDFs in **one pass**

The Gemini Decision 1 model can handle **up to 1,000 independent questions** on one shared input, returning probabilities and confidence scores in **150-250 ms** end-to-end. It costs **$0.10 per 1M input tokens**, with zero output tokens billed.

cards.camps: Some commenters call it overpriced versus Liquid; others like its audio and video inputs and report strong results in their own tests.

comments.text: I'm sort of surprised it took Jev for everyone to realize "oh yeah, this is a useful thing that we should have in our product portfolio". cards.title: Lock Your GitHub Actions

depth.text: someone made GitHub Actions easier to read by pairing **version tags** with a checked-in **lockfile**

The `gh actions-lock` extension records each action’s **commit** in `.github/workflows/actions.lock`; a **CI check** can verify the file is current and the pins still verify upstream. The zizmor maintainer says reusable workflows still need **manual SHA pins**.

cards.camps: Some praise lockfiles as a long-awaited improvement but point out gaps; others say running third-party GitHub Actions is not worth the risk.

comments.text: The advice here is really great (as I'd expect from Hugo), but as the maintainer of zizmor I want to note some caveats with the current iteration of workflow lockfiles: - They only lock normal action calls. If your workflows invoke other reusable workflows, you need to keep those hash-pinned manually for now. - Composite actions are not themselves locked. Instead, they get locked transitively…

Quoting someone else's blog I've forgotten but you're trading the trust in the repo owner not moving a tag for trusting whoever merges the commit hash to have checked that's a release in the repo you want and not _some_ forks commit. All forks on github are the same repo you can pin any commit, merged upstream or not. IMO Github should make Immutable tags mandatory to publish on…
I think my main advice is to avoid GH actions at all, unless avoiding them is somehow painful. There is just a long bad history here.

I undrrstand this looks cleaner and more intuitive, but you still have the risk of running a workflow with malicious/compromised actions, like manually, or locally with act, if you do not verify the lockfile as part of the workflow or preceded by an extra workflow step. This should be something that the runner ideally should handle (as part of the platform). This still is a workaround, just like…

Are people finding a real need for importing and updating git actions? Aren't they usually just running a one line bash command? I'd just copy paste the action in to your config so it's fully locked and under your control rather than importing some opaque script from a no name github user.

comments.text: Doesn't credit the original creator at all in the actual website?

1) It does too much too quickly. There's no acclimatisation ramp. 2) The examination area's too small. Almost every document is too large & has multiple pages. Navigation through documents is broken, with some not draggable back to the booth if clicked on. 3) Question responses are likewise too small for their dialogue boxes. They need to be in one box, either with larger boxes or smaller fonts.

I found the document management way too confusing. There's no clear game loop and I'm kinda lost what signatures mean, what the other documents are what success is. Papers please has a much simple mental model.

The primary game mechanic of stamping 'Pass' to fail a funding application is a bit confusing; should label that stamp 'Fail'/'Decline'/'Deny' or even 'Do not fund'. Pass as in to 'pass on the opportunity to fund' i.e. to not agree to fund, is not the same as Pass as in 'passed the criteria for funding' i.e. to agree to fund. To many people, Pass and Fail are antonyms, not synonyms.
Would be interesting if we could plot the average amount of time spent on the creation of showhn stuff that gets to the front page, over the past years.

cards.title: We need more goat sacrifices

depth.text: an essay says **social programs** often flop because **good intentions** aren't proof they'll work

Adam Mastroianni points to **school grants** that did nothing and **cash-transfer studies** with null or negative results. He argues that we need to check whether programs work and try again, rather than give up on **more experiments**.

cards.camps: Two camps: Critics say the essay is too gloomy and skips successful interventions; others say failed programs often reflect political motives, bad design, or missing evaluation rather than limits of social science.

cards.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG

depth.text: Apple researchers trained **small networks** to help RAG searches find the **right documents faster**

They train **SupportNet** to route queries toward promising clusters and **KeyNet** to rewrite queries toward likely matches, using examples from the query distribution. On Natural Questions, KeyNet reached 99% recall in **0.23 ms versus 1.8 ms** for raw queries; SupportNet hit 95% routing recall about 1.9× faster than centroid routing.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says learned retrieval is mainly useful at hyperscale; others prefer BM25 or grep, or say retrieval bias can hurt the LLM’s answers.
entities: Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions

comments.text: Just yesterday I saw a talk from Spotify where they presented their own fast retrieval mechanism "Parallel Fusion Router" [1]. It's also in the "learned retrieval" paradigm - in their case they use a teacher LLM to train a much smaller router LLM how to retrieve, using an LLM-as-a-judge based reward function. From my own experience, these learned methods from Apple, Spotify and others, are highly…

I feel like retrieval approaches, despite how good your ranking mechanisms are, end up biasing LLMs into what a heuristics-based system with way worse understanding of the domain says. I guess is a trade off between speed and quality, but letting the LLM explore without a bias (based on my personal experience) seems to generally provide much better results in terms of quality for the final output.

I'm not sold; that's not to say I can't be swayed, but I've spent a lot of time building RAG solutions as a "one-size-fits-all" against codebases and I am not convinced embedding models or any of the myriad BERT implementations work well enough that they can beat out grep. Most embedding/BERT models are far too small to truly grasp the nettles when an AI ask questions to them; and if you…

Apple has a fascinating history of waiting and seeing how a market develops before entering with a better product and eventually dominating, the iPod and iPhone are two examples. It seems they may be building a strong position to pull that off again in the personal assistant AI category ChatGPT is trying to dominate. I enjoy watching the slow burn approach Apple is deploying as they quietly gear…
as a recovering RAG-enthusiast, I will share a quote from a peer that has really stuck with me: "why not use grep?"

cards.title: Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint

depth.text: Firefox is making more users **look alike** to trackers, making browser **fingerprinting harder**

The study used measurements from **nearly 25 million Firefox users**. Firefox limits screen-resolution details and can report processor counts as **4 or 8**. Its evaluation found fewer **unique fingerprints** and larger groups of users sharing one.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters want tighter limits or per-site permission for fingerprinting data; another argues sites need those signals to fight bot abuse.

comments.text: I think it's great that Firefox is finally doing more to combat fingerprinting. For a long time, they lagged a bit behind Brave in this regard. Or anonymise it and replay the code before sending the request. Of course, there are legitimate use-cases…
Too bad they still generate a random unique ID for each installed extension that can expose a trackable UUID... https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1717671

One caveat I’ve experienced with Firefox branches that focus on privacy is I get “punished” with captchas from hell because I refuse to let websites siphon and prey on every last bit of private info. Hopefully this doesn’t succumb to the same issue.

I'd like to have some of the APIs that read the data used to fingerprint browsers be behind a confirmation dialog per site similar to allowing popups or microphone/video access. > Oh, I see that you'd like to read the canvas pixel data, let me check if that's okay with the user first.

glossary.export controls: Rules that limit where a company can sell certain goods, often for security reasons.
glossary.dual-class share structure: A setup where some shares give their owners more votes, helping founders keep control.
glossary.AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
glossary.flight aggregator: A service that gathers flight listings from different sources so you can compare and book them.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.multimodal: Able to work with more than one kind of input, such as text and images.
glossary.closed-set decision: A choice from a fixed list of allowed answers, rather than a free-form reply.
glossary.confidence score: A number meant to show how likely a system thinks an answer is right; it does not mean the system feels sure.
glossary.forward pass: One run through a model to produce an answer, rather than building it one piece at a time.
glossary.calibration error: A measure of how far a system's confidence is from how often its answers are actually right.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.OCR: Optical character recognition: software that reads words from a picture or scanned page.
glossary.Perl: A programming language people use to write instructions for computers.
glossary.SIGBOVIK: The event where this paper was accepted for publication.
glossary.NDA: Non-disclosure agreement: a promise not to share certain information, often because of work.
glossary.keyman risk: The risk that a company would be badly affected if one important person left or could no longer do the job.
glossary.dual-class voting rights: A setup where some shares give their owners more say in company decisions than other shares.
glossary.on-device AI: AI work that runs on your own computer instead of being sent elsewhere.
glossary.MCP server: Model Context Protocol server: a computer that lets an AI connect to outside tools or information.
glossary.open weight LLM: Large language model: an AI that works with text; “open weight” means its learned model files are made available so people can run the model themselves.
glossary.whisper.cpp: A tool that turns spoken audio into text, used here for meeting transcription.
glossary.Electron: A tool for making desktop apps with web technologies, so a web-style app can run like a regular computer program.
glossary.diarization: Working out which speaker said each part of a recording.
glossary.open-source: Software whose code is shared publicly so people can inspect it, change it, or build on it.
glossary.input-output tables: Tables that track what industries buy from and sell to one another.
glossary.ordinary pay: Hourly pay for private-payroll workers who aren't managers or supervisors, compared with the cost of things other than housing.
glossary.ticket: The author’s name for wages giving people a share of what the economy makes, since most people need a job to get money.
glossary.labor supply effect: A change in how much people choose to work when their income changes; here, people with extra money worked a little less.
glossary.Red Queen's Race: A race where everyone has to keep improving just to avoid falling behind.
glossary.lockfile: A file that records the exact versions or commits a project uses, so changes can be checked.
glossary.SHA pinning: Using a commit ID to choose an exact version instead of relying on a tag that could be moved.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: automatic checks that run when developers change code, helping catch problems early.
glossary.reusable workflow: A workflow file that another workflow can call to reuse its steps.
glossary.YC: Y Combinator: a group that gives young startups funding and advice.
glossary.term sheet: A document that spells out the main terms of an investment deal.
glossary.agent session: A saved work thread from a coding AI, including what you asked it and what it tried.
glossary.agent harness: The surrounding software that runs an AI agent and helps manage its work.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.end-to-end encryption: A way of scrambling synced information so only the people using it can read it.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.RCT: Randomized controlled trial: a way to compare a program with a similar group that did not get it, to see whether it made a difference.
glossary.null effect: A study found no clear difference between the people who got a program and those who didn't.
glossary.Goodhart's law: When a measure becomes a target, people may game it, so it stops telling you what you hoped to learn.
glossary.preregistered: A study whose researchers wrote down their plan before it began, making it harder to change the plan after seeing the results.
glossary.RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: a way for an AI to look up material and use it when answering.
glossary.MIPS: Maximum inner product search: a way to find which stored item best matches a search query.
glossary.SupportNet: A neural network that estimates how well the best item in each group matches a query.
glossary.KeyNet: A neural network that predicts which stored item is the best match for a query.
glossary.IVF: Inverted file index: a search setup that groups stored items so it can check a smaller part of the database first.
glossary.centroid: The center point used to represent a group of data.
glossary.amortization: Spreading the cost of something over time in accounting, instead of counting it all at once.
glossary.BM25: Best Matching 25: a common search formula that ranks pages by how well their words match a query, while accounting for page length.
glossary.grep: A tool for searching files for text that matches a pattern.
glossary.embedding: A set of numbers that gives an AI a way to represent a word or piece of text and how it relates to others.
glossary.browser fingerprinting: A way websites combine details about your browser and device to recognize you across sites, even without cookies.
glossary.OHTTP: Oblivious HTTP: A way to send web requests through separate services so the app server doesn't learn the sender's IP address.
glossary.telemetry: Information a program sends back about how it is being used or whether it is working properly.
glossary.private equity: Investment firms that buy whole companies, try to make them earn more, then sell them.
glossary.credit default swap (CDS): Credit default swap: a contract that offers protection if a borrower fails to repay debt.
glossary.hyperscaler: A company that rents servers and computing power at huge scale.
glossary.index fund: A fund that owns a group of investments meant to track a particular market list.
glossary.training data: The examples and text used to teach an AI system how to respond.
glossary.read-only: You can look at the information, but you can’t change it or add anything.
